> one possible way of accomplishing the resolution of the deserializer is to use a registry in the form of an Event on the MessagePort

In the browser, structured clone is used for IndexedDB and History state in addition to postMessage. [[Serializable]](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/structured-data.html#serializable-objects) platform objects are supported by all of them (if not entirely consistently across browsers). Is this idea about extending the message channel API only or is the goal to extend structured clone in general?

Side question: In HTML, “transfer” is a special case of “clone” where “[the object is] not just cloned, [but also becomes] no longer usable on the sending side”. Is this the same meaning intended by JsTransferable / kTransfer?

Node.js itself presents a solid set of use cases here. Take AbortSignal, for instance. It already inherits from EventTarget. In order to make it cloneable as has been discussed in another issue over in the dom repo, we also have to make it have the JSTransferable in it's prototype chain. We accomplish it by creating the AbortSignal first, then actually creating an instance of JSTransferable then setting *its* prototype to the AbortSignal. It ends up being largely transparent to the user but it's really a bit of a hack. Given that many of the Web Platform APIs are implemented in JavaScript in Node.js that becomes the only way we currently have to make them cloneable or transferable. Because we're creating a native object, there's also a performance penalty. It would be great if we could avoid that. 

The other use case is the known issue that JS class instances can't currently be cloned. Sure we could require that every application come up with it's own intermediary format for any JS class object they might want to clone but it would be nicer if we made it a bit easier for them -- and doing so in a way that would work consistently across multiple javascript runtimes by baking it into the standard. Basically, I'd like to be able to create a cloneable JavaScript class that works with structuredClone and postMessage no matter what platform the code is run in.

I don't understand the applicability of your first paragraph to the HTML and DOM Standards. How Node.js chooses to implement those specs has nothing to do with whether the specs make these things clonable, and in general implementation limitations or choices should have no bearing on standardization or use case discussions.

So it sounds like this reduces to making something about user classes nicer. Can you state that in the form of use cases that have come up concretely, like the example in the FAQ entry I linked to?
Note that there seems to be some demand for this [on the TC39 side](https://github.com/tc39/ecma262/issues/2555) so proxy objects can be serialized, which seems like a legitimate use case.

> Note that there seems to be some demand for this on the TC39 side so proxy objects can be serialized, which seems like a legitimate use case.

I think Mark in that thread would probably prefer that Proxies be treated like other objects (i.e. iterate the properties and serialize the values, plus a little complexity around arrays and stuff), rather than explicit support for serializing them in any special way. (That's also my preference, full disclosure.) So I don't think this should count as a use case for the purposes of this thread, necessarily.

@bakkot That is also what I’d like to see re: proxies, both to close the Proxy-exotic-object-status observability hole it creates and because there are already user-code-invoking paths (including getter invocation) so it seemingly(?) isn’t accomplishing anything useful. (Likewise “value is an Array exotic object” → `IsArray(value)`).

Regarding the proposed idea itself, I’m still pretty curious if the concept would be [specific to messaging](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/7428#issuecomment-997289077). We currently use a “descriptor wrappers” pattern towards these ends sometimes with History. A well-known-symbol contract sounds like an appealing alternative, but I’m not sure how (or if) the premise could really work in that context.
@bakkot wouldn't that mean you can still sniff out proxies from sets or platform objects and such?
I see, that seems like a relatively straightforward change then. Nice.
I just found my self in need of cloning a custom built class that i wish to save in IndexedDB

Think it would be handy if we could 1) clone something into a (shared)ArrayBuffer or Blob, 2) Send it via some api to NodeJS / Deno / Bun.js / WebRTC peer to peer 3) And then serialize it back from some binary data as a way to replace JSON that loses some information when you for example convert a Date into a String. 
`JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(new Date())) -> "not the same thing"`

JSON can't handle binary data very well it lacks support for stuff like: circular ref pointers, Blob, File, Set, Map, BigInt, TypedArrays, ArrayBuffer, Date, and everything else that structuredClone [supports](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Web_Workers_API/Structured_clone_algorithm#supported_types) 

JSON is fairly limited to what you can do with it. I think It's time to replace the old legacy JSON api with something newer that dosen't need to convert images to base64 and also have the potential to decrease the payload with something more compact.

> Think it would be handy if we could 1) clone something into a (shared)ArrayBuffer or Blob

I think you're more so asking for: #3517

no progress but the demand is greater and greater these days ... [my proposal](https://github.com/whatwg/streams/issues/1314) was to add `Symbol.clone` that acts ust like `toJSON`.

I don't have strong opinion on the `Symbol.clone` name, it could be as well more verbose as long as something makes it possible to `postMessage` proxies without breaking or requiring manual intervention from users.

Thanks for considering any progress around this topic, it's essential also in WASM related projects and specially when WASM code runs in Workers.

> We could even imagine something a bit less dynamic if that would help implementations by having an explicit register step (as previously suggested by @Ginden) akin to how customElements.define works:

Explicit registration step, using either strings or symbols stored in global symbol registry, is the only solution that I can think of that would reasonably satisfy following constraints:

* Allow multiple libraries to happily coexist within single application.
* Allow restoring from external disk in [server context](https://nodejs.org/api/v8.html#v8serializevalue).
* Allow later retrieval by changed code (what if you store your object in IndexedDB, and it's restored by different code?)

Just registering `Point` is not enough, because receiving side can't identify that `Point` class matches `Point` on sender side - duplicated class names are pretty common.

> Just registering `Point` is not enough, because receiving side can't identify that `Point` class matches `Point` on sender side - duplicated class names are pretty common.

I wasn't suggesting using the class name whatsoever, rather the prototype itself is the registry key.

Yes my suggestion doesn't support storage, i.e. it only supports postMessage/structuredClone similar to other non-storage types (`SharedArrayBuffer`, `MessagePort`, etc), but has the advantage of being able to deserialize in the agent cluster without registering per agent (i.e. `structureClone.register` would allow the engine to prepare the deserializer in whichever agents it wants).

FWIWI I don't think registering is helpful + if it uses global symbols it still collides. In my specific use case proxies in a realm don't actually want/need or *can't* be deserialized, they are forwarded back (Atomics + Proxy) so that serialization is all it's needed.

Once serialization can return something else compatible with the *structuredClone* algorithm I think it'd be up to the user / developer to decide what to do with that serialized data. automagic deserialization looks more dangerous than useful to me as it requires registering things twice per each realm and if the registration is not aligned who knows what happens while if there is just enough control to decide what to send in a `postMessage` related dance we should be good, as we've been good to date using just `toJSON` for more complex use cases/data.

Another day in WASM / JS interop, another issue to tackle around this topic.

First of all, I read again the whole thread and I think we don't strictly need `Symbol.serialize` **and** `Symbol.unserialize`, let me expand on this: the same way `toJSON` has been already good to solve similar cases, the `fromJSON` dance is an implementation detail of the receiver of the data.

Having just "*a say*" around how stuff should be passed along when `postMessage` happens, as example, and in deeply nested data, would save tons of CPU cycles for whoever, like me, needs to traverse simple to complex data trees to find out if something is **a Proxy**, and proxies are the most common identity anyone could find in the WASM / JS interop world: they proxy internal WASM pointers to the JS world and that's the story, no strings attached.

The moment any of those proxies need to survive a `postMessage` dance is the moment:

  * each WASM targeting project/PL needs to provide some *ffi* to deal with those proxies so that "*something could be done*" but it's not clear if that *something* would be better done in their code, rather than in consumers' code
  * when things run in Web Workers due potential blocking nature of most WASM targeting things, those proxied identities are super frequent in the data tree that needs to travel back and forward
  * if JS was stuck in ES3 times, with just object literals and arrays, things would be relatively simple ... today we have other primitives such as *Map* or *Set* and *Proxy* and knowing when/how to crawl their internal data just keeps piling up in terms of shipped code, logic, compromising size and performance all over the Web using these primitives

Accordingly, I would suggest to focus solely on a `Symbol.structuredClone` (no hard opinion on the name) that allows WASM targeting projects as well as JS targeting libraries to define how some specific *Proxy* or special class should travel across realms.

Thanks in advance for eventually considering that part in particular and hopefully moving forward this still open requirement for the Web platform.
I'm opposed to making this available only for Proxies. That will lead to people using them where not otherwise necessary just so they can customize cloning, which would be bad.

@bakkot I am not opposed to you being opposed to my latest idea, I am just out of ideas/use cases to present to eventually move this forward anyhow so I am trying to stretch the goal ... let's scratch that *Proxy* only idea already but please let's try to figure out a way forward around this issue, thank you!

**edit** ... cause if anyone sees that happening, people using proxies just to have this ability, it **means** this ability is more than desired so please let's find a way forward!
I agree this would be nice but alas I do not personally have the time to push for anything concrete here.

@bakkot fair enough ... now, imagine I could patch globally `postMessage` so that it crawls any crawl-able reference before actually posting data and if it finds a `Symbol.clone` method in any reference it invokes it so that we can have a real-world implementation of this idea for tests and stuff ... would that help moving this topic forward? If it does, I'm pretty quick at "*monkey patching the world*" so just let me know, thanks.

I went ahead and created a polyfill based on previous code that automatically patches `structuredClone` and `postMessage` in either the main or worker thread: https://github.com/WebReflection/symbol-structured-clone#readme

I am not suggesting anyone to use this in production but it surely shows that it is possible to have this feature and if it would be backed into the specs and accepted as new symbol by TC39 too it *could* be a polyfill to use until all vendors are aligned.

Note that if `Symbol.structuredClone` already exists, the little code that patches the world does literally nothing. I find that name pretty explicit and convenient but if there's any interest in moving this forward and a different name is used, please let me know and I'll just update the polyfill.

Thanks again for eventually considering this hugely desired improvement to the Web platform.

My personal use case for this would be to be able to add my own custom primitives that can be passed along between `postMessage()` for Web Workers.

Right now, I'm using my own custom `class Int8 extends Number { }` class which adds what would be an `int8` number type to JavaScript (in my use cases, I need to preserve the original precision of specific number types on an object, with regards to what the user set them to originally, and using `number` on it's own isn't specific enough, because that would be `float64` essentially).

Right now, when passing my `Int8` instance to the worker with `postMessage()`, the resulting object is just a plain `number` type again, it loses the branding of the type it's meant to describe.

It seems there is some confusion about where structured cloning is applied. Here's a summary:

| API | Browser | Node | Real-time |
|--------|--------|--------|--------|
| `global.structuredClone()` | ✅  | ✅  | ✅ |
| `postMessage()` | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| `History` API | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| `IndexedDB` | ✅ | ❌  | ❌ |
| [`v8.serialize`](https://nodejs.org/api/v8.html#v8serializevalue) | ❌ | ✅ | ❌ |

**Note:** Structured cloning in some cases (e.g., `IndexedDB`) is **not real-time serialization**. The deserialization of an object can occur much later — hours, days, months, or even years—potentially with a completely different codebase than the one used during serialization. We all do refactors, don't we?

Embedding a module as a "custom deserializer" can turn reflected XSS vulnerabilities into persistent XSS whenever such an object is retrieved from IndexedDB (not to even mention overhead of storing potentially tens of thousands of modules).

Deserialization seems to be much harder to achieve securely.

@Ginden fully agree on:

> a completely different codebase than the one used during serialization. We all do refactors, don't we?

but it's off this thread, where the question was: "*can we have a toJSON or toBSON (another industry standard baased on this pattern) like approach for StructuredClone operations?*"

Like it is for both `toJSON` (years of usefulness) and `toBSON` (a clear demand from the Web) the answer to the question "*how would I serialize it back in 10 years?*" remain, but it's all solvable by versioning and hints from your implementation, among raw data decoding as headers of your artifacts, same way old binary standards survived to date.

I am particularly keen to this topic these days more than ever, because while my *structured-clone* polyfill is one of the most downloaded things at runtime these days, I am working on a [buffered-clone](https://github.com/WebReflection/buffered-clone#readme) alternative that could `postMessage` *buffers* of recursive-aware cloned data, or even fill *SharedArrayBuffer* reference when desired, plus it would play perfectly fine, if not overly-fine, with anything *WASM* related.

This detail is going to be shaped as a `toBufferedClone` *symbol* if nothing happens in here, but because I need that "*yesterday*" I hope the desire and need is clear and a "*work in progress*" before I land my own thing that is as fast as *structuredClone* once hot and 3X faster than *BSON* or as fast as my *structured-clone* polyfill, except it's better on recursion, final buffer compression size, and whatnot this *API* can't, and apparently won't, provide.

To whom it might concern, I've formalized my latest proposal as [@ungap/serialization-registry](https://github.com/WebReflection/serialization-registry#readme) with a whole `@ungap/serialization-registry/polyfill` variant that automatically provides what's been proposed in all global context and through the same logic.

The current `Transfer` idea has been implemented via *Error* class and its `cause` field so that the *Error.message* carries the unique identifier and `cause` carries the transformed data that will be *revived* on the other hand (if registered).

I do think `Transfer` should be a *Blob* like opaque membrane that can be resolved only if its associated unique identifier is registered on the current receiver but due lack of similar classes in the current *JS* world I kept it simple abusing the error.

The data is never patched more than once, it's recursive friendly and it doesn't really slow-down anything but if this proposal was natively available we won't need to crawl data manually (and recursively), we would just add a single hook into the *structured clone* algorithm as it is and a fairly simple to implement one.

This proposal would solve almost everything I need for cross worlds communication (FE, BE, IoT) where the "almost" is represented by the fact that if we could have well known *Symbol* compatible too (that is `Symbol.iterator` and other global symbols reflected in every realm by specs) we could create wonders via the current primitives ... wonders that instead need monkey-patching all over the place due lack of away to intercept data that's hostile to serialize for the current algorithm status.

Thanks for considering this proposal and please let me know if I should formalize it even better or elsewhere.

Examples and details are all in the current repo 👋

Feel free to redirect if there's a better place for this, but I wanted to throw in my 2 cents, and acknowledge the great work @WebReflection has done championing this issue.

My request is slightly different.

What I'd love to see is a way to **swap the structuredClone algorithm out entirely** when interfacing with (for example) web workers and indexedDb, etc.

Structured clone is great for some use cases, but in my experience is almost always the performance bottleneck when trying to move a non-trivial amount of data across a boundary.

The amount of engineering that has gone into making structuredClone a one-size fits all solution is incredible, but at the end of the day, a recursive/iterative/exploratory implementation will always be slower than a hand-rolled implementation.

I created a micro-benchmark to show how [dramatic](https://bolt.new/~/mitata-lpp5e92c) the difference can be.

Is this the right place to have this discussion? Or is this already possible, and I missed it?

@ahrjarrett can't you replace / wrap the calls to do your own transforms? At the extreme you can write your own serialization into an ArrayBuffer and transfer that (along with any other objects that need to be transferred).

I don't know if an API to enable this more seamlessly would buy you much more.
@mhofman I can explore that option. I was hoping a more naive solution (hardcoding a cloning function) would be possible, since it feels more direct, and could be derived from a spec/schema.

> you can write your own serialization into an ArrayBuffer and transfer that (along with any other objects that need to be transferred).

that's what we do indeed to accomodate Atomics but there is a tiny caveat there: `File` is resolved synchronously in *structuredClone* algo while userland cannot be synchronous and having to resolve *some* data asynchronously kills entirely recursive serialization performance ... which is a bit of a bummer, reason some file cannot be trashed into a shared/static buffer and be happy about it.

> > you can write your own serialization into an ArrayBuffer and transfer that (along with any other objects that need to be transferred).
> 
> that's what we do indeed to accomodate Atomics but there is a tiny caveat there: `File` is resolved synchronously in _structuredClone_ algo while userland cannot be synchronous and having to resolve _some_ data asynchronously kills entirely recursive serialization performance ... which is a bit of a bummer, reason some file cannot be trashed into a shared/static buffer and be happy about it.

Can't you write everything into an `ArrayBuffer` except for `Blob`s/`File`s?

The reason they can't be serialized synchronously in userland is because for filesystem-backed `File`s, the browser does not store the byte array with the file contents, but either a path to the FS or a file handle. Letting userland read, and especially write, that, might be a privacy and security risk.

> Can't you write everything into an ArrayBuffer except for Blobs/Files?

we cover 100% of the JS types: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Web_Workers_API/Structured_clone_algorithm#javascript_types

we cannot cover 100% of the Web/API types though: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Web_Workers_API/Structured_clone_algorithm#webapi_types

In those cases we either hold a ref (proxied and managed via FinalizationRegistry as pointer) which *might* make things super slow (i.e. processing AudoData in workers when the request is synchronous and handled via SharedArrayBuffer + Atomics) or we store in IndexedDB and pick up later so that while your concerns might be valid, there are workarounds to pass that stuff around anyway, because IndexedDB supports the same algorithm anyway, it's just awkward to provide a 1:1 Atomics based API that doesn't need to retain foreign references elsewhere, in an environment already secured by all the paranoid headers and things needed to have SharedArrayBuffer work anyway 🤷

@jasnell While that does not solve the issue of standardization, isn't it already possible to pass special handling on to the user (or runtime) in the specific case of v8/node?

As far as I see, v8 by default detects only native objects to run `WriteHostObject` for, but allows customizing this behaviour with `v8::ValueSerializer::Delegate::IsHostObject`, which (when enabled by `HasCustomHostObject`) can mark arbitrary objects as "HostObjects". That would not only simplify the circumstance you described but allow writing an API for users to register their own (de-)serialization on e.g. their own classes.
